There is a much deeper history of “AI-like” thinking than most people realize.

The important distinction is that ancient and 19th-century authors did not have the modern term “artificial intelligence.” The term itself belongs to the 20th century. But people were writing about artificial beings, mechanical minds, autonomous machines, machine evolution, artificial voices, and the possibility that machines could eventually surpass humans centuries earlier.

Here is the historical trail I found.

1. Ancient Greece — intelligent machines appear in Homer

This is probably the oldest material that is genuinely relevant.

In Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, there are descriptions of artificial mechanisms created by Hephaestus that behave in surprisingly autonomous ways.

Modern scholars have explicitly analyzed these as early representations of machine intelligence. Oxford's AI Narratives: A History of Imaginative Thinking about Intelligent Machines has an entire chapter titled “Homer's Intelligent Machines: AI in Antiquity.” It examines automata, autonomous vehicles, artificial servants, and the distinction between artificial and human intelligence. (OUP Academic)

Even more striking, another scholarly work, Artificial Intelligence in Greek and Roman Epic, examines Pandora, Hephaestus's automated devices, Talos, artificial beings and Pygmalion's artificial woman specifically through the lens of AI and artificial life. (Google Books)

So we can say:

The idea of creating something artificial that imitates life is at least ~2,500 years old in Western literature.

But this is mythological AI, not technological AI.

2. Medieval period — artificial beings and artificial intelligence

The idea didn't disappear.

Medieval European traditions contain stories about artificial beings and attempts to manufacture something resembling a living intelligence.

The modern historical literature identifies traditions surrounding:

the Golem

the legendary mechanical/android figure associated with Albertus Magnus
Roger Bacon's brazen head
alchemical attempts to create artificial life
mechanical and magical artificial servants
Oxford's historical survey specifically has chapters on “Demons and Devices: Artificial and Augmented Intelligence before AI” and “The Android of Albertus Magnus: A Legend of Artificial Being.” (OUP Academic)

Again, these aren't computers. But the underlying question is remarkably familiar:

Can humans manufacture something that performs functions normally associated with intelligence or life?

3. 1200s — Al-Jazari's programmable-looking automata

This gets particularly interesting because we move from mythology toward actual engineering.

The Islamic Golden Age produced sophisticated mechanical automata. Al-Jazari, around 1206, documented machines in his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices.

His devices included elaborate water-powered mechanisms, programmable musical automata, clocks and mechanical servants.

Modern histories of artificial beings specifically trace the development of robotics from the Hellenistic period through Islamic engineering and into modern robotics. One scholarly history describes approximately 2,000 years of sophisticated automata preceding modern robotics. (Springer)

This is an important distinction:

Al-Jazari wasn't building AI.

He was building mechanical systems capable of executing predefined behavior.

That is conceptually closer to automation than modern AI.

4. 1700s — the machine-human question becomes philosophical

This is where the story becomes much more interesting.

European philosophers increasingly began asking whether human intelligence itself could be understood mechanically.

That question eventually becomes one of the intellectual foundations of AI.

The mechanical view of the human being became especially prominent during the Enlightenment. If the human body could be understood as a machine, the obvious next question was:

Could a sufficiently complicated machine reproduce human capabilities?

That question is remarkably close to the philosophical problem AI researchers still debate.

5. 1863 — Samuel Butler essentially predicts machine evolution

This is one of the most important discoveries for your question.

Samuel Butler published an article called:

“Darwin Among the Machines”

in The Press newspaper in Christchurch, New Zealand, on June 13, 1863. (Original Sources)

This is extraordinary.

Butler took Darwin's recently published theory of evolution and asked:

What happens if machines themselves evolve?

He argued that technological development might eventually produce machines that become increasingly independent and powerful.

He even contemplated machines becoming a successor species to humanity.

This isn't simply a prediction that "robots will exist."

It's an early discussion of:

machine evolution → increasing autonomy → machine superiority → humans potentially becoming obsolete.

That is astonishingly close to some modern AI-risk arguments.

And Butler wasn't finished.

6. 1872 — Erewhon and “The Book of the Machines”

Butler expanded his ideas into his 1872 novel ** Erewhon **.

Within it is a section called “The Book of the Machines.”

The premise is extraordinary: machines should potentially be regarded as evolving systems, much like biological organisms. (Text Aural)

Butler asks essentially:

If machines continue improving themselves, why should humans assume that we will remain the dominant intelligence?

That is a question you could put into an AI-safety conference today and nobody would find it strange.

The terminology is different.

The technology is different.

But the philosophical problem is remarkably similar.

7. 1909 — E.M. Forster's The Machine Stops

Then we get another surprisingly modern prediction.

E.M. Forster published ** The Machine Stops ** in 1909.

Humans live underground in isolated rooms, with virtually every need supplied by an enormous Machine.

The people become so dependent upon it that they effectively worship it and lose the ability to function independently.

The story explicitly explores what happens when humans become dependent upon the technology they created. (AERO Commons)

And that connects directly to the argument we were discussing earlier:

The danger isn't necessarily that the machine becomes evil. The danger may be that humans become incapable of functioning without it.

That's extremely relevant to today's generative AI.

8. 1943 — the mathematical foundation of neural networks

Now we're getting into actual scientific AI.

In 1943, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts published:

“A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity.”

They developed a mathematical model in which networks of simplified artificial neurons could perform logical operations. (DOI)

This is one of the foundations of what eventually became artificial neural networks.

So there is a fascinating progression:

mythical artificial beings → mechanical automata → machine evolution → mechanical brains → mathematical artificial neurons → modern AI.

9. 1948 — Norbert Wiener's Cybernetics

Norbert Wiener's ** Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine ** appeared in 1948.

This was hugely influential.

Wiener wasn't simply asking whether machines could calculate.

He was investigating control, communication, feedback and behavior in animals and machines.

The original 1948 edition is now available through MIT Press's open-access edition. (MIT Direct)

This is another major bridge between biology and machine intelligence.

10. 1949 — Giant Brains; or, Machines That Think

This one is particularly useful for what you're researching.

Edmund C. Berkeley published:

Giant Brains; or, Machines That Think

1949

The book literally opens with the question:

“Can machines think?”

Berkeley describes the new electronic calculating machines as “mechanical brains” and discusses their ability to calculate, reason, handle information and solve problems. (Project Gutenberg)

And here's something particularly interesting:

He didn't just discuss their capabilities.

He discussed their limitations and potential social consequences.

So by 1949, the discussion had already moved beyond:

“Can we build machines?”

toward:

“What happens when machines acquire increasingly sophisticated cognitive abilities?”

The complete book is available through Project Gutenberg. (Project Gutenberg)

11. 1950 — Turing asks the famous question

Then comes Alan Turing's famous 1950 paper:

“Computing Machinery and Intelligence”

It begins by asking:

“Can machines think?”

Turing deliberately replaces the difficult philosophical question with his famous imitation game, which became known as the Turing Test. (OUP Academic)

This is arguably the moment where the question becomes recognizably modern AI.

And notice the historical progression:

Homer: Can artificial things behave like living things?

Butler: Could machines evolve?

Forster: Could humans become dependent on machines?

Berkeley: Can machines think?

Turing: How would we determine whether machine behavior is intelligent?

Modern AI: We're actually building systems capable of increasingly sophisticated language, reasoning and generation.

That's one hell of a historical arc.

The most fascinating part

AI suddenly appeared in 1956.

That's technically reasonable if we're talking about the formal birth of the academic field—the Dartmouth workshop—but intellectually it's incomplete.

The idea of AI is much older than AI technology.

Humanity has repeatedly imagined the same basic progression:

1. Create artificial things.
↓
2. Make them imitate life.
↓
3. Make them perform human tasks.
↓
4. Make them reason.
↓
5. Make them autonomous.
↓
6. Make them improve.
↓
7. Wonder whether they'll surpass us.
↓
8. Worry about what happens to humans afterward.

That pattern appears repeatedly across thousands of years of literature and philosophy.

And modern scholarship explicitly recognizes this continuity. Oxford's AI Narratives describes its purpose as tracing the history of imaginative thinking about intelligent machines from ancient Greece to modern AI, including concerns about mind, creativity, power, rights and technophobia. (OUP Academic)

What if our machines become an evolutionary successor to us?

“We've been warned before.”

Not by ChatGPT.
Not by Silicon Valley.
Not by Elon Musk.

By writers and thinkers who lived long before modern AI existed.

The state-of-the-art IT infrastructure at the GMPL Yard has been conceptualised, established and enabled by CWC, integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI), digital technologies and advanced IT systems to enhance operational efficiency, security and real-time visibility of yard activities. CWC will manage and operate the yard, overseeing container handling and movement, truck entry and exit, surveillance, tracking and other technology-enabled operational functions.

A key highlight of the facility is the *Real-Time Digital Twin of the Yard and Containers*, providing a dynamic digital representation of the physical yard and enabling real-time visibility of container positions, movements and yard activities. This technology is aimed at strengthening operational control, facilitating informed decision-making and improving the overall efficiency and transparency of yard management.

tweets.text:
US CPI Policy Implications: Given that oil and distillate prices have meaningfully accelerated into September and are likely to be passed downstream to consumers, the combined August Producer Price, and Consumer Price Indices demand action out of the Federal Reserve at its next meeting. 

The combination of war induced energy shock, tariffs resulting in higher inflation and the draw upon commodities and finished goods to support the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure are all pushing the price level higher.

So why is it time for the Fed to rip up the textbook on looking through a wartime caused supply shock?

The three supply shocks have endured long enough now in their various forms that is no longer appropriate to identify them as transitory and look through them.

It is because one can observe the price of distillates such as gasoline, diesel prices and jet fuel that are rising sharply and not being absorbed via firm margin compression. 

One can plainly observe those price increases showing up in items such as groceries and everything touched by transportation and deliveries that are at the core of the American service-based economy.

I want to be clear here that the Fed should not be chasing volatile energy prices. That is not why we think the Fed should and will hike rates at the September meeting.

Rather the best monetary policy is forward-looking and seven months into what was thought to be a short-term conflict has simply turned into something else which now requires a rational policy response from the Federal Reserve.

The Fed needs to remove the three rate cuts that they implemented in late 2025 and slow an economy that is likely to grow well above trend in the current quarter, nominal GDP was above 6% in the second quarter, the deficit to GDP ratio is above 6%, the economy resides at or near full employment and in the second quarter experienced a record period of corporate profits. By slowing the economy down the central bank will force those price increases that are now flooding into household balance sheets back on to corporate balance sheets via margin compression in a policy shift aimed at providing relief to consumers experiencing an affordability crisis.

Granted that all of this is a difficult judgement-based call and is truly a coin flip at this juncture. However, following the August PPI and CPI data and what will be not a disinflation friendly PCE for the Fed not to hike rates at its next meeting would be a blow to its own credibility given clear pricing dynamics following comments by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at Jackson Hole and other rhetoric by both hawks and doves across the central bank in its aftermath.
